## Introduction

Every AI tool you have used so far --- Copilot, Antigravity, Claude Code --- locks you to one company's models. [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/) does not. It is a **router**: one account and one key, with hundreds of models behind it. To use a different model, you type a different name.

###

OpenRouter matters for two reasons.

**Money.** The cheapest good models cost about a hundredth of what the famous ones cost. For most of your work they are good enough.

**Habit.** If you only ever use one model, you start to think that model *is* AI. Once you have switched models a few times, you see it for what it is: a part you choose.

###

You will not need a credit card for anything in this tutorial. Everything here runs on a free account and free models.

The next tutorial, "Models And Money," is a different story. That one asks you to buy $10 of credits, and that does need a real card.

The companies running these free models may keep your prompts, train on them, and publish them. The model is free because **you are paying with your words instead of your money**. OpenRouter starts both switches off, so a free model refuses to answer until you turn them on.

One rule follows: **never send anything private through a free model.** No personal information, no unpublished work, no company code. Schoolwork and practice code are fine.

### Exercise 4

In the bash Terminal, set the key as an environment variable. Replace the placeholder with your actual key:

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-your-actual-key-here
```

Then run this, which prints only the first eight characters:

```bash
echo ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY:0:8}
```

CP/CR --- the second command only.

```{r}
#| label: key-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, set the key as an environment variable, replacing the placeholder with your actual key: run export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-your-actual-key-here. Then run echo ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY:0:8}, which prints only the first eight characters. CP/CR, the second command only.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
openrouter $ echo ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY:0:8}
sk-or-v1
```

###

`export` stores a name and a value in the shell's **environment**. Every program you start from that bash Terminal can read it. That is how `aider` will find your key in a minute. You never hand it over. `aider` looks up `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` by itself.

Printing the whole key would put it in your shell history and in the answers file this tutorial saves. That is how most secrets leak.

### Exercise 5

Use the key to ask OpenRouter what it knows about your account:

```bash
curl -s https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/key -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" | python -m json.tool | grep -E '"label"|"usage"|"is_free_tier"'
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: key-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "curl -s https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/key -H \"Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY\" | python -m json.tool | grep -E '\"label\"|\"usage\"|\"is_free_tier\"' CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
        "label": "sk-or-v1-2f3...4db",
        "usage": 0,
        "is_free_tier": true,
```

###

The important part of that command is `-H "Authorization: Bearer ..."`. That one line is how nearly every web API checks who you are. There is no login screen and no password box. Each request carries the key, the server checks it, and answers.

The reply comes back as **JSON**, a format that packs a lot of fields into one line. `python -m json.tool` spreads it out so you can read it, and `grep` keeps only the three lines we care about.

`usage` is `0`. You have spent nothing, and it will still say `0` when you finish. `is_free_tier` is `true`, meaning you have not bought credits. `label` is your key with the middle removed --- enough to tell two keys apart, not enough for anyone to use one.

Open a **new** bash Terminal (the `+` in the top-right corner of the Panel). In that new bash Terminal, run:

```bash
echo ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY:0:8}
```

```{.output}
openrouter $ echo ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY:0:8}

```

Empty. Your `export` only changed the terminal you typed it in. The new one started fresh and knows nothing about it.

This is the same lesson as QMD World and R World: two things running side by side do not share what you set up in the other one.

In the Dotfiles tutorial you had a variable that vanished the same way, and you made it stick by putting the `export` line in `~/.bashrc`, where every new bash Terminal reads it.

That approach would work here too, but you also know the better one: in the Dotfiles tutorial your GitHub token and your Census key went into Codespaces secrets, not files. An API key is the same kind of thing.

Take a screenshot of the **Codespaces secrets** list showing the new secret and the repository it can reach, and paste it below. The list shows names only, never the value, so the screenshot is safe to submit.

```{r}

#| echo: false
```

###

<!-- VERIFY: that a student can grant a *user* secret to PPBDS/codespace-starter, a
     public repo they do not own. If the repository picker refuses, the fallback
     is appending the export line to ~/.bashrc, and this exercise must be rewritten. -->

Your screenshot should show a secret named `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` with `PPBDS/codespace-starter` under its repository access.

###

GitHub now stores your key, encrypted, and hands it to every new Codespace you start, beside `GH_TOKEN` and `CENSUS_API_KEY`. Delete this Codespace, open a new one next week, and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is already there. You never type it again, and it is never saved in a file.

This is the line you drew in the Dotfiles tutorial, applied a third time. **Dotfiles** deliver files you wrote. **Secrets** deliver values GitHub holds encrypted, straight into the environment, with nothing written to disk. Notice that GitHub will not show you the value again either --- not even to you.

You picked `codespace-starter` because that is the repo your Codespace was built from. The machine you are sitting in belongs to it, not to `openrouter`.

One catch: GitHub only hands over secrets when a Codespace is **created**, and this one already exists. That is the rule that kept `COOLEST_TEACHER` empty until you built a new machine. Your `export` covers you for the rest of today.

### Exercise 8

Ask AI to create a `.gitignore` in your `openrouter` repo containing `.env` on its own line.

In the bash Terminal, run `cat .gitignore`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: key-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, run cat .gitignore. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
.env
```

###

`.env` is the usual name for a file that holds keys, so it is the first thing to hide from Git. You have used `.gitignore` before to keep clutter out of a repo. Here it is doing security work.

You have now used three places a value like this could live.

- **A file in the repo, hidden by `.gitignore`.** What most projects do, because the file has to sit next to the code that reads it. It holds only as long as everybody remembers. One `git add -f`, one teammate who never got told, one careless AI agent, and it is public.
- **Your private `dotfiles` repo.** This works, and plenty of professionals do it. But the key is plaintext in Git history forever, so changing it means a commit and the old one stays in the log. It lands on the disk of every machine you open. Anyone you ever add as a collaborator gets it.
- **A Codespaces secret.** Encrypted, injected into the environment when a machine is built, never written to a file. Replacing the key is one edit in one place, with no history to rewrite.

We use the secret because of that last line. A key is not a setting. It is something you will one day need to revoke in a hurry, and a Git history that keeps everything forever is exactly the property you do not want in a password.

**Settings in a repo, secrets in a secret store.** Your name and your aliases on one side, anything that can spend money on the other.

Bots scan new public commits within minutes looking for keys, and a key that reaches a public repo should be treated as stolen. GitHub tries to catch this and often blocks the push, but do not count on it.

If it ever happens to you, deleting the commit does **not** fix it. Go delete the key at <https://openrouter.ai/workspaces/default/keys> and make a new one.

## Driving A Model

You have a key that cost nothing, and `aider` will use it. In this section you find a free model, run it, and then swap in a different one without restarting.

`aider` never asked OpenRouter anything. It printed a list that was built into the program when it was released. Those four models were free once. They have all been shut down since, and starting `aider` with one gets you an error.

A tool answered instantly, confidently, and wrongly, and nothing in the output warned you.

###

Fifteen real models, and not one of them appeared on `aider`'s list. Your list will differ from ours as well. Free models come and go constantly: a company offers one to attract users, then takes it away.

Remember the command, not the names. Any tutorial or blog post that names a specific free model stops working within months.

In `google/gemma-4-31b-it:free`, `google` is the company that made it, `gemma-4-31b-it` is the model, and `:free` picks the no-cost version. The free version is the same model as the paid one. What changes is how often you may use it, and who keeps your prompts.

### Exercise 3

Pick any model from the list you just printed and start `aider` with it. We used `openai/gpt-oss-20b:free`. If yours is gone, substitute one of your own. Note the `openrouter/` on the front --- that part tells `aider` which service to route through.

```bash
aider --model openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-20b:free --no-auto-commits
```

Answer `Yes` if it offers to add `.aider*` to your `.gitignore`.

Copy and paste the banner `aider` prints when it starts.

```{r}
#| label: aider-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Copy and paste the banner aider prints when it starts.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
Added .aider* to .gitignore
Aider v0.86.2
Model: openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-20b:free with whole edit format
Git repo: .git with 0 files
Repo-map: using 4096 tokens, auto refresh
>
```

###

`aider` found your Git repo by itself and added a line to `.gitignore`. It saves its own notes in files starting with `.aider`, and it knows you do not want those committed.

Without `--no-auto-commits`, `aider` commits every change it makes for you. That is a reasonable default but a confusing one to learn with, so we turned it off. You will commit by hand at the end.

The `>` at the bottom is a prompt. `aider` is now waiting for you inside your Terminal. The slash commands you are about to type belong to `aider`, not to bash.

```{.output}
library(ggplot2)
```

A model that cost you nothing just wrote a working file and saved it. A few years ago that was a paid product.

A free model handles a two-line script easily and struggles badly with a big change across six files. Knowing which job to give which model is the skill, and the next tutorial gives you numbers for deciding.

### Exercise 5

At the `aider` prompt, run `/tokens`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: aider-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "At the aider prompt, run /tokens. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
> /tokens

Approximate context window usage for openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-20b:free, in
tokens:

$ 0.0000      471 system messages
$ 0.0000       24 hello.R         /drop to remove
==================
$ 0.0000      495 tokens total
          130,577 tokens remaining in context window
          131,072 tokens max context window size
```

###

A **token** is about three-quarters of a word. Tokens are what models read, write, and charge for. The **context window** is how much the model can hold in mind at once.

Everything in that table is sent to the model again with *every single message* you type. That is why long conversations get slower and pricier. `/clear` throws away the chat history but keeps your files.

Your file is 24 tokens. The `system messages` are 471. Before you typed anything, `aider` had already spent most of the conversation explaining to the model how to behave, and that gets re-sent every time.

The dollar column is all zeros because this model is free. On a paid model those fill in.

Switch models without leaving the session. Pick a *different* model from the live list you printed in Exercise 2, and put `openrouter/` on the front of it. At the `aider` prompt:

```default
/model openrouter/google/gemma-4-31b-it:free
```

###

```{.output}
> /model openrouter/google/gemma-4-31b-it:free
Aider v0.86.2
Main model: openrouter/google/gemma-4-31b-it:free with whole edit format
Weak model: openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-20b:free
Git repo: .git with 1 files
Repo-map: using 4096 tokens, auto refresh

```

###

One line, typed in the middle of a conversation, and you are now talking to a completely different AI from a different company. `hello.R` is still there. Google's model picked up exactly where OpenAI's left off.

The banner now shows **two** models: a *main model*, which you just changed, and a *weak model*, still the one you started with. `aider` sends the small jobs --- summarising the chat, writing a commit message --- to the cheap model, and your real questions to the main one. Using a cheap model for easy work and an expensive one for hard work is what professionals do, and here it happened automatically.

**The tool stays, the model is a part you swap.** That is why a router is worth having. Without one, trying another company's model means a new account, a new key, and a new bill.

One warning. `aider` has a `/models` command for searching model names, and it reads the same out-of-date built-in list that fooled you in Exercise 1. Use your Exercise 2 list instead.

### Exercise 7

Ask the new model a question about the code, without letting it edit anything. At the `aider` prompt:

```default
/ask What would break in hello.R if ggplot2 were not installed?
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: aider-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "/ask What would break in hello.R if ggplot2 were not installed? CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
> /ask What would break in hello.R if ggplot2 were not installed?

The library(ggplot2) call on line 1 would fail with "there is no package
called 'ggplot2'", and the script would stop there. Nothing after it runs,
so nrow(diamonds) is never reached --- diamonds ships inside ggplot2, so
it would not exist either way.
```

###

`aider` has three modes:

- `/ask` answers questions and changes nothing.
- `/code` is the default. It edits your files.
- `/architect` uses **two** models: an expensive one to plan the change, a cheap one to type it out.

That last one is the money-saving trick. Thinking is the part worth paying for. Writing out the resulting code is easy, and a cheap model does it just as well.

### Exercise 8

Leave `aider` by typing `/quit`. Then, back in the bash Terminal, check what all that cost you:

```bash
curl -s https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/key -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" | python -m json.tool | grep '"usage"'
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: aider-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "curl -s https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/key -H \"Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY\" | python -m json.tool | grep '\"usage\"' CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
        "usage": 0,
```

###

Still zero. You ran an AI coding assistant, wrote a file, asked it a question, and switched models, and it cost nothing.

There are limits. A free account gets **20 requests per minute and 50 per day**, counting all free models together. Every message you send is at least one request, and an assistant sometimes sends several for a single instruction, so 50 goes faster than it sounds.

When you run out, requests fail with `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests`. You then have three choices: wait, buy $10 of credits once to raise the daily limit to 1,000, or pay per use for a model that is not free.

"Models And Money" takes the second of those. It asks you to buy the $10, with a real credit card, because the questions it answers --- what a good model costs, and how much better than a free one it actually is --- cannot be answered on an account that has never spent anything.

## Summary

You have an OpenRouter account and an API key. Neither cost anything, and neither needed a credit card. The key is saved as a Codespaces secret, so it survives this machine being deleted and never sits in a repo.

That storage decision is the one to carry forward. The Dotfiles tutorial and this one used the same settings page for two different jobs: a repo for the settings you want to keep forever, encrypted secrets for the things you may need to revoke in a hurry --- your GitHub token there, your OpenRouter key here.

###

Along the way you learned that an `export` only affects the terminal you typed it in, that `Authorization: Bearer` is how APIs check who you are, and that a leaked key gets deleted rather than hidden.

You also ran `aider` on a free model, watched it write a file, saw how tokens are counted, and switched to another company's model mid-conversation without losing your work.

###

A model is a part with a name, a price, and a limit, and you get to choose it.

In the next tutorial, "Models And Money," you will find out what those prices actually are, why some models cost a hundred times less than others, and how to use a model from R instead of from a coding assistant.

Bring a credit card to that one. It is the only tutorial in this course that needs one, and the $10 it asks for is the whole budget.
